title: Happy Birthday to You
about: Mildred J. Hill wrote this tune for Good Morning to All, a greeting song for kindergarten classes. She published it in 1893 in Song Stories for the Kindergarten, a book she made with her sister Patty. The birthday version sung today adds two notes to its third line, with a leap of an octave.
funFact: In 2015, a US court ruled that the company charging for the birthday song had no valid copyright on its words.

practice.text: Play the right hand alone, slowly, and let the song wait for each note.
Play bars 5 to 9 with the right hand alone, where the tune jumps up high.
Put both hands together. The left hand only holds a fifth or a single note.
Play the whole song with both hands at full speed.

tips.text: The two G's at the start are long, then short. The short one leads into the next bar.
Your thumb sits on G, and each finger keeps its own key up to D.
Lift the hand after the second G, and land with the little finger on the high G.

tricky.text: Your thumb plays B, then slides down to A. Lift the hand before the two F's.
Land on the high G with the little finger, then walk down to E and C with fingers 4 and 2.
Finger 2 plays A, the thumb comes back to G, and finger 4 reaches for C.

practice.text: Play the left hand alone, and press the three notes of each chord together.
Play the waltz bass of the second verse alone: low note, chord, chord.
Join the hands on the first verse, slowly.
Play the whole song with both hands, a little slower than written.
Now play it at full speed.

tips.text: The little finger reaches a whole octave up from the thumb. The hand opens, then closes again.
After the long C, move the thumb up to G. The second verse starts an octave higher.
In the waltz bass, play the low note a little louder than the chords after it.

tricky.text: Hold the C, then move your thumb up to the next G for the second verse.
Your thumb plays B, then slides down to A, and finger 4 reaches up for F.
The thumb slides from B down to A again, now an octave higher.

practice.text: Play the Alberti bass alone until it rolls by itself: low, high, middle, high.
Play the right hand's thirds and sixths alone, and keep both notes of each pair together.
Join the hands on the first verse, slowly.
Play the whole song with both hands at three-quarter speed.
Now play it at full speed, with the pedal.

tips.text: Keep the Alberti bass soft, so the tune sings above it.
The tune is the top note of each pair, so let the upper finger lead.
The waltz bass lifts off each note. The pedal joins them, so change it at the start of each bar.

tricky.text: After the two low pairs, reach up with fingers 3 and 5 for the high D and F.
Drop the hand to the last chord: thumb on E, finger 2 on G and the little finger on C.
The pairs step down, then fingers 3 and 5 jump up to B and D.

practice.text: Play the stride bass alone: jump down for the octave, then back up for the chord.
Play the right hand's chords alone, and let the top finger sing the tune.
Play the arpeggios of the second verse in the left hand alone.
Join the hands on the whole song at three-quarter speed.
Now play it at full speed, and let the last chord ring.

tips.text: In stride, look at the octave and let the hand find the chord by feel.
Play the octaves a little apart, like bells, and let the pedal join them.
In each arpeggio, the third finger crosses over the thumb on the way up.

tricky.text: Lift the hand after the A, so it can open into the chord with F on top.
Keep the octave shape as the hand jumps up to F, and let the bass roll beneath it.
The octaves start while the left hand runs its first arpeggio. Practise each hand alone first.
